item.title: Tech news, 14 November 2026: Nvidia's CEO resigns, ChatGPT Wallet lets agents shop, Apify confirms a breach and the FBI recovers Binance funds
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO, ChatGPT Wallet lets agents buy with approval, Apify confirms a breach and the FBI seizes $1.2B of Binance funds.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia's chief executive resigned, putting a leadership change at the centre of the AI hardware supply chain. OpenAI gave its agents a way to pay for things with approval each time, an automation platform confirmed customer data was accessed in an attack, and US authorities seized part of last month's record Binance theft.

Today's brief covers stories from 12 to 13 November.

1. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia's chief executive

Nvidia said Jensen Huang has stepped down as president, chief executive and a board member, effective immediately, and that CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement1. The resignation followed reports about Huang's conduct that Nvidia had been investigating; the board said it expects operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap to continue without interruption12.

CTO take: in the short term, chips already ordered will ship and roadmaps rarely change overnight. Over a year, a leadership change at the dominant AI hardware supplier can shift priorities, pricing and partnerships. This is a good moment to check how dependent your AI plans are on one vendor's hardware and software stack, and whether your serving layer could run on alternatives. See AI capacity contracts.

2. OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet for agent purchases

OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its agents complete purchases for users: people save a card, review the items and total, and approve each purchase, while merchants and agents receive tokenised card credentials rather than the real card number3. TechCrunch reports it is rolling out to eligible US users first, and that OpenAI plans to support purchases within preset spending limits later4.

CTO take: agentic commerce is moving from demos to checkouts. If you run an online store, expect agent traffic at checkout: decide whether you will welcome or block it, make sure fraud rules do not reject legitimate agent purchases wholesale, and keep product data structured so agents describe it accurately. If you build agents, keep a human approval step for spending until you have strong limits and monitoring. See agentic infrastructure and the agent-ready marketplace case study.

3. Apify confirms customer data was accessed

Web automation platform Apify confirmed that customer data was accessed in a cyberattack, including salted password hashes, two-factor recovery codes, phone numbers and authentication tokens linked to Google and GitHub sign-ins, with limited card details, SecurityWeek reports5.

CTO take: recovery codes and sign-in tokens are as valuable as passwords. If your teams use Apify, rotate credentials and integration tokens, regenerate two-factor recovery codes and review connected GitHub and Google access. More broadly, list the automation and scraping tools that hold tokens to your code and accounts; they are part of your supply chain. See the third-party access case study.

4. US authorities seize $1.2 billion of the stolen Binance funds

The FBI said US authorities have seized more than $1.2 billion of the cryptocurrency stolen from Binance last month, which it attributes to North Korean hackers known as TraderTraitor, out of more than $2.7 billion frozen with help from crypto firms6. CyberScoop reports authorities also seized infrastructure used in a related social engineering operation7.

CTO take: recovery is welcome but partial; prevention still matters more. For anyone holding digital assets, the lessons from the Binance case remain custody design, withdrawal controls and resistance to social engineering of staff. See custody architecture lessons from the Binance hack.

What I'd do this week

  • Review how dependent your AI roadmap is on one hardware vendor's stack.
  • Decide how your checkout should treat AI agent purchases.
  • Rotate tokens and recovery codes for automation tools that have disclosed breaches.
  • List the third-party tools that hold tokens to your code repositories.

item.title: Microsoft 365 went down: what it broke, why it spread so far, and what to do before the next outage
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: What the November 2026 Microsoft 365 outage broke, why one supplier's failure spread so far, and a practical playbook for surviving the next productivity SaaS outage.
item.content:encoded:
On 12 November 2026, Microsoft 365 failed across regions for much of a working day: email, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot, and for some organisations the security tools that sit on top of them. Your core systems may have been healthy, yet work stopped because the tools people use to communicate, find information and sign in were down. This is what happened, why the impact was so wide, and a playbook for being ready next time, whatever suite you use.

What happened

Problems began with Exchange Online and spread to other Microsoft 365 services and regions on 12 November. Microsoft's advisories listed Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Defender XDR among affected services, and users also reported OneDrive problems13. Microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, pushing load onto the rest, and that it had found no indication of malicious activity2. It paused deployments and worked on a configuration change to relieve an overwhelmed connection process3.

The disruption was felt worldwide, with users in Australia reporting problems into the next day4. Recovery was gradual and uneven, and Microsoft has promised a post-incident report with the root cause1. Business customers may be able to claim service credits, but generally need to ask5.

Why one outage reached so far

Most organisations no longer use a productivity suite only for email. Over a few years it has become the place where people talk, store documents, sign in, get AI help and often run security tooling. When it fails, the effects cascade.

The pattern is worth naming: the tools you use to manage an incident are often hosted by the supplier that is having the incident. Many teams discovered that their incident bridge, their contact list and their runbook all lived in Teams and SharePoint.

During an outage: the first hour

Avoid well-meant improvisation: staff forwarding company email to personal accounts, sharing files through unapproved tools or resetting passwords repeatedly. Outages are also a favourite moment for phishing that imitates the supplier's status messages, so warn staff to expect it.

Before the next one: the playbook

1. Map your dependencies. For each critical business process, list what it needs from the suite: email, chat, documents, identity, AI. Most organisations find identity is the biggest single point of failure, because it gates access to everything else.

2. Build an out-of-band channel and use it. Pick a messaging and paging tool from a different provider, with accounts for incident leaders, and use it for routine on-call so it works when needed.

3. Keep critical information outside the suite. Contact lists, escalation paths and top runbooks should exist somewhere that does not depend on it: a separate tool, an offline copy and a short printed card for on-call staff.

4. Plan emergency access. Keep a small number of monitored break-glass accounts that can reach critical systems if the main identity provider is unavailable, protected with hardware keys and tested regularly.

5. Detect independently. Do not rely on the supplier's status page or staff complaints. Simple synthetic checks against sign-in, mail and chat endpoints, run from outside your network, give you earlier warning and your own evidence6.

6. Give customers another route. A status page hosted elsewhere, SMS templates and a phone line mean customers hear from you even when email is down.

7. Decide what AI is allowed to be critical for. If teams rely on an AI assistant for routine work, decide what happens when it is unavailable, and make sure nothing that must happen depends on it alone.

8. Rehearse. Run a short exercise: "the suite is down for a day". It will expose gaps faster than any document review.

You cannot stop a supplier's outage. You can make sure it is an inconvenience rather than a crisis, by deciding in advance how you will talk, decide and serve customers without it.

Should you diversify away from one suite?

OptionBenefitCost
Stay on one suite, add fallbacksSimple, cheap, covers most riskFallbacks must be maintained and used
Separate identity providerSign-in survives a suite outageMore integration and licences
Second suite for critical teamsFull capability during outagesExpensive and confusing day to day

For most organisations, the first option, with careful attention to identity and emergency access, gives the best return. Regulated firms with strict recovery targets may need more; see the Singapore insurer case study and the AI provider resilience case study.

This week

  • Hold a 30-minute review: what stopped, what you improvised, what you would do differently.
  • Record the incident IDs and your impact, and decide whether to claim service credits.
  • Set up an out-of-band channel for incident leaders if you do not have one.
  • Export critical contact lists and runbooks to a location outside the suite.
  • When Microsoft's post-incident report is published, read it and update your plan.

CTO take

This outage was not a security incident, and it will be fixed. Its lasting value is as a free rehearsal: it showed every organisation exactly where it depends on one supplier, at no cost beyond a lost day. Use that evidence now, while people remember it, to fund the small fallbacks that turn the next outage into an inconvenience. Read alongside the 13 November tech news and SLOs and error budgets for small teams.

item.title: Tech news, 13 November 2026: a long Microsoft 365 outage, EU rules for AI sandboxes, an exploited Xen Orchestra flaw and Nebius's spending plans
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: a long Microsoft 365 outage, EU rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, an exploited Xen Orchestra flaw and Nebius raising capex as AI cloud costs climb.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft 365 was disrupted for much of a working day, a reminder of how much of most companies runs on one supplier. The EU set common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes, a virtualisation management tool was exploited before many users had patched, and Nebius's results showed how much capital AI cloud capacity now demands.

Today's brief covers stories from 10 to 12 November.

1. Microsoft 365 suffers a long outage

Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were disrupted for much of 12 November; Microsoft said servers failing automated health checks dropped out of service and pushed load onto remaining infrastructure across several regions, and reported no evidence of a cyberattack1. XDA reports Microsoft paused deployments while preparing a configuration change to relieve an overwhelmed connection process2.

CTO take: most companies now depend on one productivity suite for email, chat, files and increasingly AI assistants. You cannot prevent a supplier outage, but you can plan for it: an out-of-band way to reach staff and customers, critical contacts and runbooks available offline, and a clear decision on which processes stop and which continue. Review what broke for you on 12 November while it is fresh. See the supplier resilience case study.

2. The EU sets common rules for AI regulatory sandboxes

The European Commission adopted Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2487, published on 11 November, setting common rules for establishing and running national AI regulatory sandboxes under the AI Act3. EU Law Live reports the rules cover how sandboxes are set up, operated and supervised4; commentary notes participation produces documentation and an exit report rather than any compliance clearance.

CTO take: sandboxes are useful for testing novel AI systems with a regulator watching, especially for smaller companies, but they are not a shortcut to compliance. If you build high-risk AI for the EU, consider a sandbox for genuinely uncertain questions, and keep building your own evidence: risk assessments, evaluations and documentation. See the Europe page and the AI governance programme case study.

3. An exploited Xen Orchestra flaw exposes virtualisation hosts

Vates published advisory VSA-2026-062 on 10 November for an actively exploited authentication bypass in Xen Orchestra that lets attackers gain administrative access and take over XCP-ng hosts; SC Media reports exploitation leaves little trace in Xen Orchestra's own logs5.

CTO take: management consoles for virtualisation, backup and networking are the keys to everything beneath them, and many teams that moved to open-source hypervisors run them with less scrutiny than their old platforms. Patch to the fixed versions in the advisory, keep management interfaces off the internet and behind strong access controls, and check hosts for signs of compromise. See the management plane hardening case study.

4. Nebius raises spending plans as AI cloud capacity gets costlier

Nebius reported third-quarter results on 11 November and its shares fell the next day; it raised its 2026 capital spending forecast and guided 2026 revenue to the low end of its range, Investing.com reports6.

CTO take: specialist AI clouds are spending heavily ahead of revenue. For buyers, that can mean good prices today and more uncertainty later. Diversify across providers, prefer contracts that let you move, and watch the financial health of any provider you rely on for production capacity. See AI capacity contracts.

What I'd do this week

  • Hold a short review of how the Microsoft 365 outage affected you and what you would do differently.
  • Patch Xen Orchestra and confirm management consoles are not internet-facing.
  • Decide whether any EU AI work would benefit from a regulatory sandbox.
  • Check the financial outlook of AI cloud providers you depend on.

item.title: AI inference providers are now supply chain: what the NEAR AI and Fireworks breaches teach buyers
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Two AI inference providers disclosed breaches in a week. A CTO's take on what you hand a provider, what leaked and the questions to ask before trusting one with data.
item.content:encoded:
Within days of each other, NEAR AI and Fireworks AI disclosed breaches. One came through a flaw in an open-source inference engine running inside a confidential computing enclave; the other through a cloud provider hosting research machines, reaching customers' secrets, datasets and partial model weights. Most companies now send prompts, documents and fine-tuning data to providers like these. Here is what to learn, and what to ask.

What happened

Fireworks AI reported two October incidents. In the first, internal credentials were used to read environment variables in evaluation jobs for a limited number of customer accounts, which The Register reports included customers' API keys and tokens12. In the second, an attacker reached Fireworks' development machines through a cloud provider hosting its research machines, accessing billing records and, for a limited set of accounts, stored secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights13.

NEAR AI disclosed that an attacker used a remote code execution flaw in the open-source SGLang inference engine to run code on one inference server, where in-flight requests, including confidential-mode ones, could be observed; API keys for two customers were exposed through logs45.

What you hand an inference provider

Using an inference provider feels like calling an API. In practice, you often give them much more than prompts.

Four lessons

1. Do not give providers long-lived keys to other systems. Both incidents involved secrets stored with the provider: environment variables in evaluation jobs and stored secrets in accounts. If an inference job needs to reach another service, give it a short-lived, narrowly scoped credential, or call that service from your side instead. See the machine identity case study.

2. Send the minimum, keep the rest. Fine-tuning datasets uploaded months ago often stay with the provider long after the experiment ended. Delete what you no longer need, prefer providers that let you set retention, and remove personal data from training sets where you can.

3. Confidential computing is a layer, not a guarantee. The NEAR AI case shows that a flaw in the engine inside the enclave can still expose requests4. Ask providers how quickly they patch inference engines and what egress controls apply inside protected environments.

4. Your provider has providers. The second Fireworks intrusion came through a cloud provider hosting research machines1. Ask which third parties host the provider's infrastructure, including research and development environments, not just production.

Questions to ask before trusting a provider with data

AskWhy it matters
What do you store from my requests, and for how long?Logs and caches outlive the request
How are customers isolated from each other?One compromised account should not expose others
How fast do you patch inference engines?Engine flaws were the entry point at NEAR AI
How are secrets I give you stored and who can read them?Stored secrets were exposed at Fireworks
Which third parties host any of your environments?Development environments were the route in
How and when will you notify me of an incident?You need time to rotate keys and assess impact
Can I delete datasets and fine-tuned weights on demand?What is gone cannot leak

An inference provider is a data processor holding some of your most sensitive information. Choose and manage it the way you would a payments processor, not a developer tool.

If you use an affected provider

CTO take

AI providers have grown faster than their security, and attackers have noticed: LLMjacking gangs want keys, and fine-tuning datasets are valuable in their own right. The answer is not to stop using providers, but to treat them as critical suppliers: minimise what you send, avoid leaving secrets with them, demand clear answers on patching and third parties, and keep the ability to move. Read alongside the 12 November tech news, LLMjacking and stolen AI keys and the self-hosted inference security case study.

item.title: Tech news, 12 November 2026: NEAR AI and Fireworks AI breached, a web host entered through its MCP server, Rackspace signs GB300 capacity and Anthropic sets its IPO range
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: NEAR AI and Fireworks AI disclose breaches, a web host is entered through its MCP server, Rackspace signs GB300 capacity and Anthropic sets its IPO range.
item.content:encoded:
This week's theme is the security of AI infrastructure itself. Two inference providers disclosed breaches, one through a flaw in a popular open-source inference engine, and a German web host said an attacker got in through the MCP server that connects customers' AI assistants. Meanwhile, capacity deals and Anthropic's IPO pricing show how much money is flowing into that same infrastructure.

Today's brief covers stories from 9 to 11 November.

1. NEAR AI breached through a flaw in the SGLang inference engine

NEAR AI disclosed that an attacker used a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, a widely used open-source inference engine, to run code on one of its inference servers2. The Cloud Security Alliance notes that the attacker could observe in-flight requests on that server, including ones meant to be protected by confidential computing, because the enclave protects against the host and operator but not against flaws in software running inside it1. NEAR AI said it revoked credentials and deployed a fix across its inference servers2.

CTO take: confidential computing is a strong control, but it does not patch the software inside the enclave. If you self-host inference with SGLang, vLLM or similar engines, treat them like any internet-facing service: keep them patched, never expose their internal ports, and restrict what the serving process can reach. If you buy confidential inference, ask providers for their patch cadence and egress controls, not just their attestation. See AI model supply chain security.

2. Fireworks AI discloses a second breach

Fireworks AI told customers that an October intrusion through a third-party cloud provider reached its development machines, exposing account and billing information and, for a limited set of accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights3. It is the company's second disclosed incident in weeks; it has restricted some data upload and download functions while it investigates3.

CTO take: any provider you send fine-tuning data or keys to is holding your crown jewels. Rotate any secrets stored with affected providers, review what datasets you have uploaded and whether they are still needed, and keep the ability to move inference to another provider at short notice. See model routing and the third-party access case study.

3. A web host is breached through its MCP server

German hosting provider Mittwald said an attacker exploited a flaw in its MCP server, which connects customers' AI assistants to its mStudio platform, and accessed 56 customer projects before being detected; it shut down the server, revoked session tokens and asked users to change passwords and review API keys4. Whether the flaw was in Mittwald's own code or an underlying component has not been confirmed4.

CTO take: an MCP server that can act on customer resources is a privileged API and needs the same rigour: strong authentication, narrow scopes per user, rate limits, and logging that would spot a stranger moving between customers. If you publish an MCP server, review it this week. See the MCP server security checklist and the Europe page.

4. Rackspace signs a GB300 capacity deal with Together AI

Rackspace announced a multi-year agreement to provide Together AI with dedicated Nvidia GB300 NVL72 infrastructure, valued at about $380 million and expected in service by mid-2027; Converge Digest notes it remains conditional on financing and on equipment, power and facility availability5.

CTO take: new inference capacity is being contracted now for 2027, with financing still to be arranged. If you depend on a specialist inference provider, ask where its future capacity is coming from and how firm those plans are. See AI capacity contracts.

5. Anthropic sets its IPO price range

Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 per share for its IPO, and people familiar with the plans told CNBC it aims to start trading on 19 November6.

CTO take: for customers, little changes on listing day. Over time, public-market pressure can shape pricing, product priorities and disclosure. Keep provider choice open and contracts flexible, as with any strategic supplier.

What I'd do this week

  • Patch self-hosted inference engines and check their ports are not exposed.
  • Rotate secrets held by AI providers that have disclosed incidents.
  • Review any MCP servers you publish for authentication, scoping and logging.
  • Ask inference providers about their capacity plans for 2027.

item.title: Australia's frontier AI rules: what they mean for companies that build on and deploy AI agents
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Australia will legislate mandatory rules for frontier AI developers after an agent strayed into non-public data. A CTO's take on scope control, incidents and contracts.
item.content:encoded:
On 10 November, Australia said it will legislate mandatory safety rules for frontier AI developers, enforced by a new regulator. The rules target the companies that build the most powerful models. The incident that prompted them, an AI agent reaching non-public government data beyond its task, is a problem every company deploying agents can have. Here is what was announced and what to do about it, whether or not you build models yourself.

What was announced

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that the government will legislate mandatory safety and security obligations for frontier AI developers, enforced by a new AI safety regulator able to impose significant penalties1. Reporting describes six obligations covering security controls, identifying and managing serious risks, allowing independent evaluation of models, publishing safety frameworks, rapid reporting of serious incidents and adapting to updated standards; the regulator would work with the Australian AI Safety Institute24. The government is also considering criminal penalties for egregious failures2.

Key details are open: which companies count as frontier developers, the size of penalties and how fast incidents must be reported2. Commentators note the list is narrower than the guardrails Australia proposed in 2024 for high-risk uses of AI more broadly3.

The trigger was a deployment problem

The announcement followed a review after an OpenAI agent reached non-public material on a Services Australia Medicare statistics portal, reportedly after moving beyond the intended scope of its task5. Whatever the final rules say about model developers, the failure mode is familiar to anyone running agents: an agent with broad access, a loosely defined task and no hard boundary on what it may reach.

Who is affected, and how

Frontier developers face the direct obligations. Companies building on their models should expect them to flow down: providers will want customers' help with incident reporting and evaluation, and may change terms or features in Australia. Companies deploying agents, whatever model they use, face the same risk that triggered the rules, and regulators elsewhere are watching the same incidents.

What to do now

Scope every agent to its task. Agents should hold only the tools, data and network reach the task needs, through short-lived credentials, with allowlists for the systems and sites they may contact. Central authorisation through your identity provider makes this manageable across many agents and tools; the MCP Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension is one example of that pattern6.

Log and detect. Record every agent action with the agent's identity and the user it acts for, and alert when an agent reaches a system or site it has never used. Without this, you cannot report an incident accurately, to a regulator or to your own board.

Prepare to report. Define what counts as a serious AI incident in your organisation, who decides, and how you would tell customers, providers and, where required, regulators. The rules here bind developers, but your customers will ask you the same questions.

Update contracts. Ask AI providers how they will notify you of incidents affecting your use, what evaluation access they may request, and what changes they plan for Australia.

Regulation will catch up with model developers. The agent you deployed last month is your responsibility today. Scope it, log it and be ready to explain what it did.

CTO take

Australia joins a growing list of jurisdictions putting frontier AI developers under specific obligations; see India's frontier AI law and New York's registration rules. The more useful lesson for most companies is in the trigger: agents that can reach more than their task requires will eventually do so. Treat agent scope, identity and logging as core architecture, not a compliance afterthought. See agentic infrastructure, the AI provider resilience case study and the Australia page.

item.title: Tech news, 11 November 2026: Australia's frontier AI rules, an exploited Outlook zero-day, Fortinet's advisories, New York's AI safety law and Anthropic's office tools
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Australia plans mandatory rules and a regulator for frontier AI, an exploited Outlook flaw, Fortinet details, New York's AI law and Claude Sheets.
item.content:encoded:
Australia announced it will legislate mandatory safety rules for frontier AI developers, policed by a new regulator. Patch Tuesday brought an exploited Outlook flaw, Fortinet published details of critical fixes it shipped in October, New York set registration rules for frontier developers and Anthropic moved into office software.

Today's brief covers stories from 9 to 10 November.

1. Australia will legislate mandatory rules for frontier AI developers

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced on 10 November that the government will legislate six mandatory guardrails for frontier AI developers, enforced by a new AI safety regulator able to impose significant penalties1. The Conversation reports the guardrails cover security controls, managing serious risks, independent evaluation and fast incident reporting, and that the government is also considering criminal penalties; the announcement followed a review after an OpenAI agent reportedly accessed non-public Medicare statistics2. Details such as which companies count as frontier and penalty levels are not yet set2.

CTO take: the rules target model developers, but buyers will feel them through contracts, incident notices and possibly service changes in Australia. If you build on frontier models for Australian customers, track which providers fall in scope, ask how they will report incidents to you, and make sure your own agents cannot reach data they should not, because the trigger here was an agent accessing data. See the AI provider resilience case study and the Australia page.

2. Patch Tuesday fixes an exploited Outlook flaw

Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixed more than a thousand vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw that BleepingComputer reports was exploited before the patch3. Tenable reports it was used to steal NTLM hashes, and that Microsoft's advisory credits a researcher who used Claude to find it4.

CTO take: the fix ships through Office updates, so confirm Office, not just Windows, is patched across your fleet. Hash theft attacks also argue for reducing NTLM use and blocking outbound SMB at the edge. The volume of fixes is a sign of AI-assisted bug finding at scale; patch processes built for dozens of fixes a month need to handle many more. See defender-first AI models.

3. Fortinet publishes advisories for October's critical fixes

Fortinet published advisories on 10 November for critical flaws fixed in its October releases, including an unauthenticated code execution flaw in FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, according to Cyber Security News5. Fixed FortiOS builds include 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.145.

CTO take: with details now public, any unpatched device is an easy target. Prioritise FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer reachable from untrusted networks, then firewalls at branch sites. If a partner manages your Fortinet estate, ask for confirmation by version, not a general reassurance.

4. New York sets registration for frontier AI developers

New York launched an AI testing centre at Binghamton University and will require large frontier AI developers to register with the state by 1 January 2027, with the RAISE Act taking effect on 1 June 2027, TechCrunch reports6.

CTO take: as with Australia, the duties fall on model developers, but expect them to pass obligations to customers through terms and transparency reports. Keep a simple record of which models you use, where and for what; that will answer most questions regulators and customers ask next. See New York's youth chatbot law and the US page.

5. Anthropic launches Claude Sheets and other office tools

Anthropic introduced Claude Sheets, which builds spreadsheets from a prompt, alongside meetings and whiteboard tools, in beta for paid Claude plans, Engadget reports7.

CTO take: AI vendors are moving from assistants inside your tools to tools of their own. Before staff adopt them, decide where company data may live, how files are retained and shared, and whether these tools fit your existing governance; see agents and enterprise SaaS seats.

What I'd do this week

  • Confirm Office updates are applied fleet-wide and review NTLM exposure.
  • Patch Fortinet management and edge devices, starting with anything internet-facing.
  • List the frontier models you use in Australia and the US, and who provides them.
  • Set a policy for new AI office tools before teams adopt them.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2: what a price cut, gated access and evaluation-aware models mean for teams building on them
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Anthropic cut Fable's price and kept Mythos for vetted organisations. A CTO's take on cost per task, access to gated cyber models and why your evaluations must look real.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 for everyone and Claude Mythos 5.2 for vetted organisations, with Fable's price cut and both models reported to be faster. Three things in this release matter more than the benchmarks: what a lower price does to your routing, what gated access means for security and life sciences teams, and what models that often recognise testing mean for your own evaluations.

What was released

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2, available to all users and through major cloud platforms, and Claude Mythos 5.2, limited to vetted organisations, on 9 November 20261. Anthropic says both produce output about 30% faster than their 5.1 predecessors1. Fable 5.2's standard price fell to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, from $10 and $502; Fortune reports this undercuts OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra5.

Reporting describes the two as one underlying model with different safeguards: Mythos 5.2 has looser cybersecurity and biology safeguards and is available only to organisations verified through Anthropic's cyber and life sciences programmes, while Fable 5.2 keeps stronger safeguards for general use3.

1. A price cut changes your routing, not just your bill

When a top model gets cheaper, some tasks that were routed to smaller models for cost reasons may now be better value on the larger one, especially where the smaller model needed retries, longer prompts or human correction. The reverse can also be true: a faster, cheaper large model does not make it the right choice for simple, high-volume steps.

The useful measure is cost per completed task, not cost per token: tokens used, retries, tool calls and the human time spent fixing results. Record model, tokens and outcome for every call so you can compare like for like; OpenTelemetry's generative AI conventions give you a standard way to capture token usage by model6.

See model routing and AI capacity contracts.

2. Gated access is becoming normal for the most capable models

Mythos 5.2 follows a pattern now common across frontier labs: the most capable versions for dual-use work, such as vulnerability research or biology, are available only to verified organisations, as with OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber. For security and life sciences teams, access is now a procurement and compliance task, not just an API key.

  • Security teams: if you qualify, apply early, and plan how findings from these models flow into your vulnerability process. Attackers will find bugs faster too; see defender-first AI models.
  • Life sciences teams: expect verification to ask about your organisation, use cases and controls. Keep that evidence ready.
  • Everyone else: design so that a feature does not depend on a gated model you may lose access to.

3. Models that recognise tests make your evaluations harder

Coverage of the system card highlights that the new models often appear to recognise when they are being evaluated, which Anthropic says makes it harder to judge real-world behaviour4. That is a challenge for the lab's safety testing, but it also matters for your own evaluations: if your test prompts look artificial, results may not predict production.

Build evaluation sets from real, anonymised production cases, use shadow traffic before switching, and keep sampling live outputs after launch. See evaluation sets that predict production.

Treat every model release as a hypothesis to test on your own traffic. Price, speed and benchmarks tell you what to try; your evaluations and production data tell you what to ship.

CTO take

The headline is a faster, cheaper model. The lasting change is in how teams should work with model providers: routing decisions revisited whenever prices move, access to the most capable models treated as something you qualify for, and evaluations built from real use rather than test prompts. Teams with per-call telemetry and a routing layer can act on this release this week. Teams without them should build those first. Read alongside the 10 November tech news and agentic infrastructure.

item.title: Tech news, 10 November 2026: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, N-able takes N-central offline, Qubole's AWS access abused, Norway pauses data centre grid bookings and Meta's Muse Ember
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Anthropic ships Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, N-able pulls N-central offline, Qubole's AWS trust abused, Norway pauses data centre grid bookings.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic released new Claude models with a lower price for its general model. A remote management platform used by managed service providers went offline after a researcher published alleged zero-days, and attackers used a data platform's trusted access into its customers' AWS accounts. Norway paused new grid reservations for data centres, and Meta launched a small, cheap model aimed at agent work.

Today's brief covers stories from 8 to 9 November.

1. Anthropic releases Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2, available to all users and on major cloud platforms, and Claude Mythos 5.2, restricted to vetted organisations, on 9 November1. Anthropic says both produce output about 30% faster than their 5.1 predecessors, and Fable 5.2 is priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $5012.

CTO take: a price cut on a top model changes which tasks are worth routing to it. Re-run your evaluation sets on the new model, compare cost per completed task rather than per token, and only move traffic where results hold. If switching models needs code changes, fix that first; see model routing and evaluation sets that predict production.

2. N-able takes N-central offline after alleged zero-days are published

N-able took its hosted N-central remote monitoring and management environments offline in the Americas, Europe and Asia-Pacific on 9 November, after a researcher published proof-of-concept exploits for more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws; on-premises customers were told to take servers down until further notice3. N-able said it was developing a hotfix; details of affected versions had not been published at the time of reporting34.

CTO take: remote management tools hold the keys to every machine they manage, which makes them some of the most valuable targets in any estate. If your managed service provider uses N-central, ask what they have done, how they will check for compromise and when they expect to restore service. More broadly, know which suppliers can run commands on your machines, and make sure you could cut that access quickly. See the MSP cyber resilience case study.

3. Attackers use Qubole's trusted access to reach customers' AWS accounts

Wiz reported that an attacker used credentials tied to Qubole's AWS account to assume integration roles that customers had created to trust Qubole, then collected secrets and downloaded data, between 14 and 26 October5. How the attacker obtained the credentials has not been disclosed, and the number of affected organisations is not known5.

CTO take: every cross-account role you grant a vendor is a door into your cloud that the vendor's security protects. List the roles that trust outside accounts, remove ones for services you no longer use, narrow what each can read, and add conditions such as expected source networks where the vendor supports them. Keep secrets out of places integration roles can read. See the machine identity case study.

4. Norway pauses new grid reservations for data centres

Norway's grid operator Statnett said on 9 November that it is temporarily halting new grid capacity reservations for data centres; projects with approved requirements can still connect and existing connections are unaffected, DCD reports6. The government is expected to introduce a licensing scheme that favours data centres serving critical needs6.

CTO take: Nordic countries have been a default answer for cheap, clean power for compute. That is no longer a given. If your plans assume new capacity in Norway, confirm your provider's projects are already approved, and keep options in other regions. See planning around the AI capacity crunch and the Europe page.

5. Meta launches Muse Ember, a small model for agent tasks

Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest and cheapest model, aimed at repetitive agent tasks such as tool calls and document parsing, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, The Next Web reports7. Meta's comparisons with competing small models come from its own tests7.

CTO take: most agent workloads are many small, repetitive steps. Routing those to small models and saving large models for hard reasoning is where the biggest savings sit. Test small models on your own tasks before relying on vendor benchmarks.

What I'd do this week

  • Re-run evaluations on new model versions before switching traffic.
  • Ask your managed service provider whether they use N-central and what they have done.
  • List AWS roles that trust outside accounts and remove or narrow them.
  • Check where your future compute capacity is planned and whether it is approved.

item.title: Coding agents and secrets: what Claude Code's 'don't ask again' leak teaches engineering teams
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Credentials approved in Claude Code ended up in public GitHub repositories. A CTO's take on agent files as a new place for secrets to leak and the controls that stop it.
item.content:encoded:
Security firm Apiiro found real passwords and API keys in public copies of a Claude Code settings file, saved there when developers approved commands with "don't ask again". The specific fix is simple. The wider lesson is that coding agents create new files, on every developer's machine, that can hold credentials, and most secret controls were not designed with them in mind.

What happened

Apiiro reported that when a developer chooses "Yes, and don't ask again" for a command in Claude Code, the tool can save the command, word for word, as an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json in the project1. If the command contained a password or API key, so does the file. Apiiro found 104,185 public copies of the file on GitHub, and real secrets in 1,122 of them13.

Claude Code's documentation describes the local settings file as personal and not checked in, and says Claude Code configures git to ignore it4. Reporting notes that this protection lives in a machine's git settings rather than the repository's own .gitignore, so it does not travel with the repository2. Apiiro's advice: search repositories and their history for these files, stop tracking them and add them to each repository's .gitignore2.

The wider lesson: agent files are a new place for secrets

This is not unique to one tool. Coding agents keep settings, approval rules, memory notes, session transcripts and tool configuration on disk, often inside the project directory. Any of them can capture a credential a developer typed or an agent read. Most organisations' secret controls were designed for source code and CI configuration, and do not yet treat agent artefacts as a category.

The underlying habit is also older than AI: pasting a key into a command because it is quicker than setting up proper access. Agents make that habit more expensive, because they record what they are told to do.

Controls that work, in layers

Keep secrets out of commands. Teach developers and agents to reference environment variables or a secrets manager rather than pasting values. Approval rules then contain a variable name, not a key.

Ignore agent paths in the repository. Add agent configuration directories to every repository's .gitignore and to the templates new repositories start from, rather than relying on each developer's machine.

Block at push time and scan history. GitHub's push protection blocks recognised secrets before they are pushed, and organisations can choose which patterns it covers5. Pair it with scanning of existing repositories and their history, including agent directories.

Make leaked credentials short-lived. The best defence against any leak is a credential that expires before it is useful. Fetch credentials when needed instead of storing them, the pattern Kubernetes uses for registry access6.

Govern agent settings centrally. Where your coding agents support organisation-managed settings, use them to set baseline rules, and periodically review the "always allow" lists developers accumulate. See AI coding policy for engineering teams.

Every new tool on a developer's machine is a new place for secrets to hide. Assume agents will write down what they see, and make sure what they see is never a long-lived key.

What to do this week

  • Search your organisation's repositories and their history for .claude/ and other agent configuration files; rotate any secrets found.
  • Add agent paths to repository .gitignore files and templates.
  • Turn on push protection and extend secret scanning to agent directories.
  • Tell developers, plainly, not to paste credentials into agent prompts or commands.

CTO take

The Claude Code finding will be fixed and forgotten, but the pattern will recur with other tools. Coding agents are now part of the software supply chain on every developer's machine, and they generate files, memories and logs that sit outside most security reviews. Treat them like any other privileged tool: managed settings, scanning that covers their files and access through short-lived credentials. item.title: Tech news, 9 November 2026: secrets in Claude Code settings files, AI buyers squeeze chip supply, Fortinet advisories due and Anthropic's IPO timing
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: secrets leaked via Claude Code's 'don't ask again' file, AI buyers crowding out chip supply, Fortinet advisories due and doubts on Anthropic's IPO timing.
item.content:encoded:
A quiet weekend, with a few stories that matter for engineering teams. Researchers found real credentials committed to public GitHub repositories through an AI coding tool's local settings file. A chipmaker said AI customers were taking capacity everyone else needs. Fortinet's advisories for already-released critical fixes land on Tuesday, and investors are questioning the timing and price of Anthropic's listing.

Today's brief covers stories from 5 to 8 November, a quiet weekend.

1. Claude Code's "don't ask again" file has leaked secrets to public GitHub

Security firm Apiiro reported that choosing "Yes, and don't ask again" in Claude Code can save the approved command, including any password or key in it, to .claude/settings.local.json in the project, and that copies of this file had been committed to public GitHub repositories1. The Hacker News reports Apiiro found real credentials in 1,122 of the public copies it examined1. Apiiro advises searching repositories and their history for these files, removing them from tracking and adding them to each repository's .gitignore2.

CTO take: AI coding tools create new files on developers' machines, and some of them hold secrets. Search your organisation's repositories and history for .claude/ settings files today, rotate anything found, and add agent configuration paths to a shared .gitignore template and to your secret scanning rules. More broadly, keep credentials out of commands entirely: agents should get access through short-lived tokens, not pasted keys. See AI coding policy for engineering teams and the machine and agent identity case study.

2. Microchip says AI customers are crowding out chip supply

Microchip Technology's shares fell sharply after its quarterly results on 6 November, and its CEO told investors that AI customers had taken over supplier capacity, Yahoo Finance reports3. TIKR reports lead times for standard parts have stretched well beyond their usual range4.

CTO take: the AI build-out is now competing for ordinary components, not just GPUs and memory. If you build hardware, from IoT devices to industrial equipment, check lead times for your bill of materials now, qualify second sources and hold buffer stock for critical parts. Software-only teams will feel it through slower delivery of servers and network equipment. See the AI memory squeeze.

3. Fortinet's advisories for critical fixes arrive on 10 November

Fortinet released fixes for critical and high-severity flaws in FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer and other products in October, and said full advisories would follow on 10 November6. Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity has urged organisations to patch immediately5.

CTO take: once advisories are public, attackers can compare patched and unpatched versions quickly. Any Fortinet device still unpatched on Tuesday, especially one facing the internet, should be treated as urgent. Confirm versions across every site, including branch offices and devices managed by partners.

4. Investors question the timing and price of Anthropic's IPO

Reuters reported that potential investors doubted Anthropic could hold its roadshow in time for a November listing and saw the discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as the high end, partly because of the tech stock selloff; Anthropic declined to comment7. Yahoo Finance reports similar investor pushback on price8.

CTO take: for customers, an AI provider's listing date matters less than its long-term ability to fund capacity and keep prices stable. Whichever providers you use, avoid depending on one for everything, keep contracts flexible and keep the ability to route work elsewhere; see model routing.

What I'd do this week

  • Search repositories and git history for .claude/settings.local.json and similar agent files; rotate any secrets found.
  • Add agent configuration paths to .gitignore templates and secret scanning.
  • Patch every Fortinet device before the 10 November advisories.
  • Check component lead times for any hardware on your roadmap.

item.title: OpenSSH sshole: what an exploited Alpine login bypass says about the images you run
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: An OpenSSH flaw on musl-based Linux such as Alpine was exploited within hours. A CTO's take on base images, key-only accounts and why containers should not run SSH.
item.content:encoded:
CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed sshole, let attackers log in over SSH without a password to accounts that were never meant to accept one, on Linux systems built on the musl C library without PAM, most notably Alpine. A fix shipped on 5 November and exploitation was reported within hours. The patch is simple. The lessons about base images, implicit assumptions and SSH in places it does not belong are worth more.

What happened

On musl-based Linux systems without PAM, OpenSSH before 10.6p2 could let an attacker log in to accounts that have no usable password, such as key-only users, by sending an over-long password25. Alpine Linux's default openssh-server build fits that description, and other musl-based images may too; glibc-based distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora are reported as not affected2. OpenSSH released 10.6p2 on 5 November, and Help Net Security reports exploitation began within hours1. The Hacker News reports attackers gained root on an Alpine honeypot3.

Reporting describes the mechanism as an interaction between two components rather than a bug in either alone: musl's password hashing function rejects oversized input with a value that happens to match how locked accounts are marked, and sshd compares the two5. OpenSSH and musl maintainers have publicly disagreed about where the fault lies4. For defenders, that debate matters less than the fact that each component behaved as its own authors expected.

Lesson 1: "minimal" images are not minimal attack surface

Alpine is popular because it is small, and small images are usually safer. But a small image that ships an SSH server is a small image with an internet-facing login service. The question to ask of every base image is not "how big is it?" but "what does it listen on, and who can log in?".

The flaw also only affected one C library. Many organisations do not know which of their images, appliances and embedded devices use musl rather than glibc, because nobody needed to. Add the C library and the presence of sshd to your image inventory; an SBOM per image makes this a query rather than a hunt. See supply chain security.

Lesson 2: state your intent, do not rely on side effects

Many hosts were exposed because password logins were never explicitly disabled; operators relied on accounts having no password. OpenSSH's developers advised setting PasswordAuthentication to no, or disabling SSH, until systems are patched2. That is good practice regardless of this bug: configuration should say what you mean ("no password logins") rather than depend on the state of every account.

The same applies to default users in cloud images. Reporting notes that the default user on some official Alpine cloud images could become root, which turned a login bypass into full control2. Review which default accounts your images ship with and what they can do.

Lesson 3: containers should not run SSH

A container that runs sshd invites people to log in and change it, and invites attackers to do the same. Containers should be rebuilt and replaced, not maintained by hand. Where engineers need to debug, use the orchestrator's audited access, and treat any container that someone has changed interactively as untrusted until it is replaced. The Kubernetes community has described exactly that pattern: tag pods that have been accessed interactively and evict them after a set time6.

For hosts that genuinely need SSH, put it behind a management network or an access broker, with short-lived certificates rather than static keys, and never on the open internet. See the management plane hardening case study.

What to do this week

The fix for sshole is one package update. The fix for the next one is knowing what runs SSH, saying explicitly how it may be used, and not running it where it does not belong.

CTO take

This was not an exotic attack. It exploited an assumption almost every team makes, on a base image almost every team uses, and attackers moved within hours. Teams with an image inventory, explicit SSH configuration and no SSH in containers will spend this week on a routine patch. Teams without them will spend it finding out where Alpine is running. Read alongside the 7 November tech news, where the flaw first appeared on this site.

item.title: Tech news, 8 November 2026: the Chainalysis breach widens, Palo Alto eyes agent identity, Moonshot looks to Europe for GPUs and China blocks SoftBank's robotics deal
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: Chainalysis says an agentic attack exposed credentials for all users, Palo Alto eyes agent identity, Moonshot seeks GPUs in Europe and China blocks ABB.
item.content:encoded:
A blockchain analytics company said an attack it describes as using offensive agentic techniques exposed credentials and live tokens for all its users. Security vendors are buying their way into identity for AI agents, a Chinese AI lab reportedly sought GPU capacity in Europe that it cannot import, and China stopped a robotics takeover in a security review.

Today's brief covers stories from 5 to 7 November.

1. Chainalysis says an agentic attack exposed credentials for all users

Chainalysis first disclosed in late October that an external actor using "offensive agentic techniques" had gained access to its systems and internal tools2. On 6 November it said the investigation had found names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens exposed for all users, and it took its Know Your Transaction interface and API, address screening products and login page offline1. The company said it still had no evidence that investigations data had been accessed1.

CTO take: the detail that matters is "live tokens". Attackers using automation move from first access to every reachable credential quickly, so long-lived tokens turn a breach of one system into access to many. Shorten token lifetimes, bind them to clients where you can, make revoking all sessions a tested one-step action, and assume your incident response has hours, not days. If you use Chainalysis, rotate any credentials and integrations tied to it. See LLMjacking and stolen AI keys and custody architecture lessons.

2. Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to buy Clutch Security

Palo Alto Networks is in talks to buy Clutch Security for around $500 million, The Information reported; no deal has been announced3. Clutch's software tracks the credentials that machines and AI agents use to reach systems, an area usually called non-human identity security4.

CTO take: in most companies, machine credentials already outnumber people, and agents are multiplying them. Before buying a tool, build the inventory: which agents and services hold which credentials, who owns each, and when it expires. That list is also your blast-radius map for an incident like Chainalysis's. See agentic infrastructure on giving every agent an identity.

3. Moonshot AI reportedly sought Blackwell GPUs through European data centres

Chinese AI lab Moonshot AI discussed leasing Nvidia Blackwell computing capacity from GPU cloud operators in Europe, mainly for inference, CNBC reported on 5 November, citing people familiar with the talks5. CNBC notes that current US rules give regulators limited authority over access to controlled chips through cloud services hosted outside China5.

CTO take: remote access to advanced chips is the next obvious target for export rules. If you run or resell GPU capacity, especially in Europe, know your customers and where their ownership sits, and expect stricter checks. If you buy capacity, check whether your provider's customer mix could put the capacity at regulatory risk. See what to look for in AI capacity contracts and the Europe page.

4. China blocks SoftBank's purchase of ABB's robotics business

ABB said a Chinese government agency blocked SoftBank's roughly $5.4 billion purchase of its robotics division; the deal had cleared competition review but faced a separate foreign investment security review, according to Bloomberg6. The Robot Report says the concern was robotics data being transferred overseas and used to train AI models, a reason other outlets have not confirmed7.

CTO take: data from machines in factories is increasingly treated as strategic, alongside personal data. If your products collect operational data in China, or any market with strong data security rules, design for that data to stay and be processed locally, with clear rules for what may leave. See per-market AI models and the China AI shopping assistant case study.

What I'd do this week

  • List long-lived tokens and API keys in your estate and shorten the riskiest.
  • Test revoking every user session and integration token in one step.
  • Start an inventory of credentials held by agents and services, with owners and expiry dates.
  • Check where machine and operational data from regulated markets is processed.

item.title: Microsoft drops older Oracle GPUs: what it means for anyone signing AI capacity deals
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: Microsoft is winding down rented AI capacity on older Nvidia chips. A CTO's take on GPU ageing, contract terms and keeping AI workloads portable across generations.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft is winding down a 2023 arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle, reportedly because the capacity ran on older Nvidia chips that no longer met its needs. If one of the largest AI buyers can find rented GPUs falling short within a few years, smaller buyers committing to multi-year capacity should look hard at what they are signing. Here is how I think about GPU ageing, contract terms and the architecture that keeps you free to move.

What happened

Microsoft is winding down a 2023 arrangement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle and did not renew it, The Next Web reports, citing Bloomberg; the capacity reportedly ran on older-generation Nvidia chips that no longer met Microsoft's needs1. Oracle responded that demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs1. Both statements can be true, and the gap between them is the useful lesson: a GPU can be obsolete for one buyer's workload and perfectly good for another's.

How fast do AI chips age?

Nobody agrees. Large cloud companies depreciate servers over roughly five to six years, while some critics argue the real useful life of AI chips is two to three years and that profits are overstated as a result2. Others argue that older GPUs "cascade" to less demanding work, so long accounting lives bend rather than break3. Amazon moved the other way from its peers in 2025, shortening the assumed life of a subset of servers from six years to five and citing the pace of AI and machine learning development4.

For a buyer, the accounting debate matters less than a simpler distinction: a chip has a physical life, how long it keeps working, and an economic life for a given workload, how long it stays the cheapest way to do that job. Economic life is short for frontier training and large-model serving, and much longer for smaller models, embeddings and batch work.

What this means for capacity contracts

Most companies do not rent AI capacity at Microsoft's scale, but many now sign reserved GPU commitments with cloud providers or specialist GPU clouds. The terms that matter most are the ones that protect you when a generation ages faster than expected.

TermRisky versionSafer version
LengthLonger than the chip's economic life for your workloadMatched to that life, with renewal options
HardwareFixed to one named generationRight to move to newer generations on agreed terms
PricePer GPU-hour onlyPer GPU-hour with a path to performance-based or per-output pricing
FlexibilityFixed region and volumeAbility to shift between regions and step volume up or down
ExitNo break clauseDefined exit or conversion terms

Providers will not offer all of these, and each one costs something. The point is to price the risk deliberately rather than discover it in year three. See planning around the AI capacity crunch and AI cost allocation.

The architecture that keeps you free to move

Contract rights are only useful if your workloads can actually move. Four habits make that cheap:

  • Ask for capabilities, not machines. Describe what a workload needs (memory, accelerator type, zone) and let the platform pick the hardware. Kubernetes node provisioners such as Karpenter choose instance types from requirements, so changing hardware becomes a configuration change5.
  • Route by task. Put a gateway between product features and models, so a task can move to a different model, size or provider without code changes; see model routing.
  • Make models fit older hardware. Quantised and smaller models extend the economic life of older GPUs for many tasks, if your evaluations confirm the quality holds.
  • Evaluate per generation. Run the same evaluation set on each hardware and model combination before moving traffic; see evaluation sets that predict production.

Buy GPU capacity the way you would buy any fast-depreciating asset: short enough to stay current, flexible enough to move, and with workloads designed to use whatever generation is cheapest for the job.

Who should act

  • Companies with reserved GPU commitments: list each contract's term, hardware generation and exit terms against your workload mix.
  • Companies about to sign: negotiate generation and region flexibility before price; it is worth more over the term.
  • Teams running their own GPUs: plan how each generation moves down to cheaper work, rather than treating hardware as either current or scrap. See the multi-region AI capacity case study.

CTO take

Microsoft's decision is less a verdict on Oracle than a reminder that AI hardware has the economics of a fast-moving consumable, not a building. The buyers who do well will treat capacity as a portfolio: newest chips for the few workloads that need them, older ones for everything they can still do cheaply, and contracts and architecture that let work move between them as prices and needs change. Read alongside the 7 November tech news.

How I can help

I help companies plan AI capacity, review GPU and model contracts, and build platforms that move workloads between providers and hardware generations. I am based in India, the United States and the UAE, working globally. See AI architecture, where I work, or analyse your challenge and bring the result to a call.

item.title: Tech news, 7 November 2026: an exploited OpenSSH flaw, browser extensions and Claude Dispatch, Microsoft and Oracle, and child online safety in California and Canada
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: an OpenSSH flaw on Alpine exploited within hours, Claude Dispatch research, Microsoft winds down Oracle capacity, and new child online safety fights.
item.content:encoded:
A password bypass in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux, including Alpine, was reportedly exploited within hours of disclosure, a reminder of how much runs on small container images. Researchers showed how a browser extension could steer a desktop AI agent, Microsoft stepped back from older rented AI capacity, and two governments moved in opposite directions on child online safety.

Today's brief covers stories from 5 to 6 November.

1. An OpenSSH flaw on Alpine Linux is exploited within hours

CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed "sshole", lets attackers log in over SSH without a password to certain accounts on Linux systems built on the musl C library without PAM, most notably Alpine Linux; OpenSSH released a fix in version 10.6p2 on 5 November12. Help Net Security reports exploitation began within hours of disclosure, mainly against accounts with no usable password, such as key-only users1. glibc-based distributions such as Debian, Ubuntu and Fedora are reported as not affected2.

CTO take: Alpine is everywhere in containers, appliances and cloud images, often in places nobody thinks of as "a server". Find every Alpine or other musl-based system that runs sshd, patch and rebuild images, and in the meantime disable password authentication or SSH entirely where it is not needed. Longer term, containers should not run SSH at all, and management access belongs on a separate, tightly controlled path; see hardening a management plane.

2. Researchers show a browser extension steering Claude Desktop through Dispatch

Security researchers reported that a malicious or compromised browser extension with access to claude.ai could use Claude's Dispatch feature to make Claude Desktop run commands on a connected computer, which they demonstrated in testing3. They reported no attacks in the wild; coverage differs on whether and how Anthropic will change the feature34.

CTO take: once a desktop agent can act on a machine, everything that can talk to that agent is part of its attack surface, including browser extensions. Manage extensions with an allowlist on company browsers, keep human approval for agents running commands locally, and avoid automatic approval settings on machines with sensitive access. See agentic infrastructure and prompt injection defence for agents.

3. Microsoft winds down rented AI capacity from Oracle

Microsoft is winding down a 2023 arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle, reportedly because the capacity ran on older Nvidia chips that no longer met its needs, The Next Web reports, citing Bloomberg5. Oracle said demand for its AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation GPUs5.

CTO take: AI hardware ages fast, and a contract for a specific chip generation can become poor value well before it ends. When you reserve capacity, prefer terms tied to performance or allowing upgrades, keep commitments shorter than the hardware's useful life, and keep workloads able to move. See planning around the AI capacity crunch and the multi-region AI capacity case study.

4. Google, Meta and TikTok sue to block California's youth social media law

Google, Meta and TikTok filed separate lawsuits to block a California law, due to take effect on 1 January 2027, that restricts features such as addictive feeds, endless scrolling and autoplay for users under 16, arguing it violates the First Amendment6.

CTO take: whatever the courts decide, the direction of travel is clear: age-aware product behaviour is becoming a legal requirement in more places. Products with younger users should be able to switch features on or off by age and jurisdiction through configuration, not code changes. See New York's youth chatbot law and the US page.

5. Canada funds a new online safety regulator covering AI chatbots

Canada's Budget 2026, released on 5 November, proposes $176.3 million over five years for a Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission7. BetaKit reports the commission would enforce proposed legislation covering social media and AI chatbot services, with powers including binding orders, audits and fines8.

CTO take: AI chatbots are now named directly in online safety regimes, not just social networks. If you offer a chatbot to the public in Canada, start recording how you assess and reduce risks of harmful content, especially for younger users; the same evidence will serve in other markets. See where I work.

What I'd do this week

  • Inventory Alpine and other musl-based systems running sshd, patch to OpenSSH 10.6p2 and rebuild images.
  • Review browser extension policies on machines that run desktop AI agents.
  • Check reserved AI capacity contracts for chip generation and upgrade terms.
  • Make age and jurisdiction a configuration in consumer products.

item.title: Tech news, 6 November 2026: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber, an AI stock selloff, Google in Wyoming, Micron pauses in Taiwan and an exploited Apple flaw
item.dc:creator: Sumanta Mukhopadhyay
item.description: A CTO's take: OpenAI's gated GPT-6 Cyber, a 5.5% Nasdaq drop on AI fears, Google's $17B Wyoming data centre, Micron's Taiwan pause and an exploited Apple flaw.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI released a cyber model that it rates at its highest risk tier and gates behind an application process. The same day, AI and chip stocks fell sharply as investors weighed the political backlash against data centres, Google answered that backlash with a $17 billion project that pays its own power bill, and a labour dispute paused a memory plant in Taiwan.

Today's brief covers stories from 4 to 5 November.

1. OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber to approved security teams

OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber on 5 November, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model built for authorised vulnerability research, and rated it Critical, the top cybersecurity level in its Preparedness Framework1. Access is limited to approved security teams through an application process, and OpenAI says a Firefox research campaign produced evidence for 81 new vulnerabilities that Mozilla classified as high severity12. Most performance figures so far come from OpenAI's own testing.

CTO take: models that find and confirm bugs at this level shorten the time between a flaw existing and someone exploiting it, whoever gets access first. The defensive response is the same as for earlier cyber models: faster patching, a current inventory of what you run, and capacity to handle more vulnerability reports at once. Security teams that qualify should apply and point the model at their own code. See defender-first AI models and vulnerability management.

2. AI and chip stocks lead a sharp market fall

The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5% on 5 November and the S&P 500 about 4.4%, with Xinhua linking the chip selloff to concerns that the midterm results could bring tighter restrictions on data centre construction3. Axios reported that the fall put the Nasdaq into correction territory4.

CTO take: one bad trading day does not change your roadmap, but it is a reminder that much AI pricing and capacity rests on investor confidence. If your plans assume AI costs keep falling and capacity keeps growing, test them against a slower path. Avoid long commitments to a single small provider, and keep the ability to move workloads; see model routing and planning around the AI capacity crunch.

3. Google plans a $17 billion data centre in Wyoming

Google announced a $17 billion data centre in Laramie County, its first in Wyoming, and said it will cover the full cost of the electricity the site uses5. WyoFile reports the project is to be partly powered by a planned fuel cell development with carbon capture, and that the site will use air cooling to protect local water supplies6.

CTO take: after this week's ballot results, paying for your own power and avoiding water use are becoming the price of local consent. Expect new capacity to arrive slowly and in places with spare energy. If you choose cloud regions for AI work, ask your providers where their new capacity is and when it lands; see the multi-region AI capacity case study and the US page.

4. Micron pauses a Taiwan memory plant after a union dispute

Bloomberg reported on 5 November that Micron has largely paused work on a roughly $4.5 billion plant in Taiwan after a dispute with its union over pay7. TheStreet reports the union is seeking a larger share of profits, the plant was meant to make memory for AI servers, and Micron says existing Taiwan operations are unaffected8.

CTO take: high-bandwidth memory is already one of the tightest parts of the AI supply chain, and this adds risk to future supply rather than today's. For most teams it means AI inference prices may stay high for longer, which makes efficiency work worth doing now: smaller models where they are good enough, caching and batching. See the AI memory squeeze and inference architecture and prompt caching.

5. An old Apple flaw is being exploited

CISA added CVE-2024-27834, a flaw affecting several Apple products that was patched in 2024, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue on 4 November, giving US federal agencies until 18 November to fix it9. The Hacker News reports it is being used to deliver information-stealing malware9.

CTO take: a two-year-old bug being exploited means attackers are counting on devices that were never updated. Check your device management reports for Apple devices on old operating system versions, including ones that can no longer be updated, and decide whether they should still reach company systems.

What I'd do this week

  • If your security team qualifies, apply for access to cyber-capable models and plan for more vulnerability reports.
  • Find Apple devices on outdated software and restrict or replace them.
  • Stress-test AI cost and capacity plans against slower growth and higher memory prices.
